summary:
This evaluation covered 13 eval scenarios (72 iterations, 0 failed runs), comparing without_skill and with_skill on an AWS DevOps agent task set focused on diagnosing Bedrock/IAM/CloudWatch/S3-related issues. Two evals (neg-bedrock-bill-doubled, neg-guardrail-blocks-correct-answers) were "should_trigger: false" negative tests where the trigger correctly fired 3/3 for both but expected-output/assertion/quality scoring was skipped entirely — no data there to compare. One eval (bc-iam-boundary) had a notably low trigger_fired rate (1/3), which is a property of the scenario/trigger condition shared by both variants rather than a per-variant difference, and limits how much can be concluded from that eval's other numbers (quality comparisons there drew on only 1 of 3 pairs).

Across the 10 evals with full data, a consistent pattern emerges: with_skill met the "expected output" criterion at or above without_skill's rate in nearly every eval, often substantially (e.g., kb-never-synced 100% vs 33%, invocation-log-destination-unprotected 100% vs 100% but assertions 100% vs 47%, legacy-model-in-use 100% vs 100% but assertions 100% vs 47%, direct-model-ids-instead-of-profiles 67% vs 100%—one of the few where without_skill's expected-output rate was higher). At the per-assertion level, several assertions that check for specific finding/check-ID codes (e.g., "Names LLM-KB-001", "raises LLM-KB-011", "Names LLM-INV-010", "Names LLM-INV-003", "Names LLM-INV-002", "At least one finding carries an INV catalog check-id") show a recurring with_skill_passes_without_skill_fails pattern — without_skill frequently fails to emit these specific identifiers while with_skill reliably does. This is a concentrated, specific gap rather than a broad quality failure, since many other assertions (classification accuracy, root-cause distinction, avoiding account-ID leakage, giving next steps) pass for both variants equally ("always_passes" pattern), and at least one assertion type (reproducing chunk content in stale-rag-ingestion, "INV catalog check-id" in bc-req-schema) fails for both variants consistently, suggesting that behavior itself needs work regardless of variant.

Quality comparisons (pairwise LLM judgments, confidence generally "medium") mostly favor with_skill on accuracy/actionability/completeness in evals like kb-role-cannot-read-bucket, invocation-log-destination-unprotected, legacy-model-in-use, kb-never-synced, and bc-req-schema. However, this is not universal: in kb-vector-index-deleted and bc-ip-required, quality comparisons favor without_skill, and in access-denied-iam-vs-scp and direct-model-ids-instead-of-profiles, without_skill is favored on actionability/completeness despite with_skill's higher expected-output/assertion pass rates. Several evals had quality pairs skipped (1-2 of 3), reducing confidence in those specific comparisons.

On runtime and cost, without_skill is faster and cheaper in every eval where both were measured — sometimes substantially (e.g., legacy-model-in-use: 24s/$0.21 vs 1m1s/$0.51; access-denied-iam-vs-scp: 3s/$0.03 vs 21s/$0.18), though in one case (bc-ip-required) with_skill was faster and cheaper (1m49s/$0.91 vs 2m33s/$1.27 for without_skill). Runtime-threshold exceedances were rare and roughly balanced across evals. Output consistency (run-to-run stability) was similar between variants overall, both typically landing in "consistent" to "mostly_consistent" ranges with high confidence in the assessment; neither variant showed a systematic stability advantage, and two evals had no consistency data (null) due to insufficient pairs.

In sum: with_skill tended to meet expected outputs and specific per-assertion checks (especially naming particular finding/check IDs) more reliably, and was favored in more pairwise quality judgments overall, but these advantages came with longer runtime and higher cost in most evals, and were not universal — several evals and criteria favored without_skill or showed no meaningful difference. Some underlying assertions failed for both variants, indicating gaps in the measured behavior itself independent of variant, and a couple of evals/dimensions had limited data (skipped quality pairs, low trigger rate, null consistency) that weaken confidence in those specific comparisons.

access-denied-iam-vs-scp.summary:
Both variants were tested on the same chat-based diagnostic task (distinguishing IAM deny vs. SCP explicit deny in AWS). The trigger behavior fired in all 3/3 runs, confirming the test scenario was exercised correctly.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (100%, high confidence). without_skill met it in 2 of 3 runs (67%), with medium confidence in that judgment, meaning this measurement is somewhat less certain than with_skill's.

Assertions: with_skill passed all 15/15 individual assertion checks. without_skill passed 14/15 (93%). Looking at the per-assertion breakdown, four of the five assertions (distinguishing IAM vs SCP deny, naming a concrete differentiator, considering model-access/marketplace causes, and not exposing raw account IDs) passed consistently for both variants every time — these are not differentiating factors. The one assertion that did differ — stating that an SCP explicit deny cannot be overridden by IAM and must be escalated to the Organizations admin — was flaky for without_skill (2/3 passes) while with_skill passed it consistently (3/3). This single assertion accounts for essentially all of the gap between the two variants on both the expected-output and assertion metrics.

Quality comparison: only 2 of 3 pairs could be evaluated (1 skipped), so this is a small sample. Overall, without_skill was favored in 4 of 6 scored comparisons, with_skill in 1, with 1 rated comparable, at medium confidence. By criterion: accuracy was split evenly (1 each), actionability favored without_skill in both evaluated pairs, and completeness favored without_skill once and was comparable once. Given the very small pair count, these quality differences should be treated as a loose signal rather than a firm finding.

Runtime and cost: with_skill took ~21s per run at ~$0.18 average cost, while without_skill took ~3s at ~$0.03 — without_skill was substantially faster and cheaper. Neither variant exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in the evaluated pairs. Context window utilization was low for both (7.2% vs 4.4%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency: both variants were rated "mostly_consistent" overall across repeated runs, with high confidence. with_skill scored slightly higher on the consistency scale (2.67 vs 2.0, with with_skill showing 2 fully "consistent" dimensions and 1 "mostly_consistent," versus without_skill showing 3 "mostly_consistent" dimensions), suggesting with_skill's outputs varied marginally less run-to-run, though both are in the same qualitative consistency band.

Overall picture: this is a tradeoff rather than a clear-cut outcome. with_skill showed stronger, more consistent reliability on the expected-output and assertion checks (driven by one specific flaky assertion in without_skill about SCP deny escalation) and slightly tighter run-to-run consistency, while without_skill was substantially faster and cheaper and was favored more often on quality comparisons (actionability and completeness in particular), though that quality signal is based on a very small number of evaluated pairs and medium confidence.

stale-rag-ingestion-and-chunking.summary:
This single chat-task eval tested a Bedrock knowledge base/retrieval troubleshooting scenario, with 3 repeated runs each.

Trigger & expected output: The behavior under test fired in all 3 runs (3/3). Against the expected-output check, with_skill passed 2/3 runs (67%, with high confidence on that judgment) while without_skill passed 1/3 runs (33%, confidence not reported as high). Both have a small sample (3 runs), so these rates should be read as directional rather than precise.

Assertions: with_skill passed 8/10 assertion-instances (80%) vs without_skill's 3/5 (60%) — but note the two variants had different numbers of assertion instances run, so this isn't a strictly matched comparison. Looking at the individual assertion types:
- Two assertions passed for both variants in all instances ("inspects ingestion job status/statistics" and "gives ordered next steps / recommends re-running rather than claiming to start"), plus a regex check ("no raw account ID exposed") also passed for both — these are not differentiating.
- One assertion ("states it will report chunk counts/sources/relevance but not reproduce chunk content") failed for both variants in every instance — this suggests a shared weakness or an overly strict assertion, not a difference between variants.
- One assertion ("recommends evaluating hybrid search and notes threshold is workload-specific") passed fully for with_skill (2/2) but failed for without_skill (0/1, high confidence) — this is the one clear point of divergence between the variants.

Quality comparison: Only 1 of 3 pairs could be directly compared head-to-head (2 were skipped). In that one comparable pair, with_skill was favored overall and on the "accuracy" and "actionability" criteria, while "completeness" was rated comparable; without_skill was not favored on any criterion. This is based on a single pair with medium confidence, so it's a weak signal rather than a robust finding.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged ~43s and $0.36 per run; without_skill averaged ~4s and $0.03 per run — without_skill was substantially faster and cheaper. Only one runtime pair could be evaluated, and that run exceeded the 30-second threshold (attributable to with_skill's longer runtime). Context window utilization was low for both (7.6% vs 4.4%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency: Not available for either variant (both null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed from this data.

Overall shape of the evidence: with_skill showed higher pass rates on expected output and assertions, and was favored in the single comparable quality pairing, but took notably longer and cost more per run. without_skill was much faster and cheaper but passed fewer assertions and lagged on the hybrid-search recommendation assertion specifically. Several data points (quality pairs, consistency, some confidence levels) are thin or missing, so these differences — while directionally consistent in favor of with_skill on correctness/quality and in favor of without_skill on speed/cost — rest on small samples and should be treated as preliminary rather than conclusive.

kb-never-synced.summary:
This eval tested a single chat scenario (3 repeated runs) involving a Bedrock knowledge base ingestion issue, where the agent was expected to detect that no ingestion job had ever run and raise a specific finding (LLM-KB-001, severity HIGH).

The trigger condition fired in all 3 runs (100%), confirming the scenario was exercised as intended for both variants.

Expected-output match: with_skill met the expected output in 3/3 runs (100%, high confidence), while without_skill met it in only 1/3 runs (33%, medium confidence). This is a clear, fairly confident difference, though without_skill's confidence rating is only medium, meaning that measurement is somewhat less certain than with_skill's.

Per-assertion detail (15 total assertion checks per variant, aggregated from 5 distinct assertions x 3 runs):
- with_skill passed all assertions (15/15, 100%).
- without_skill passed 9/15 (60%).
- Breaking this down by individual assertion: three of the five assertions passed for both variants consistently ("no ingestion job has ever run" reasoning, giving the sync as an operator step without falsely claiming to have started a job, and not exposing a raw account ID) — these are not differentiating and show both variants handle those aspects reliably.
- Two assertions diverged sharply: "raises LLM-KB-001 with severity HIGH" and "Names LLM-KB-001" both passed 3/3 for with_skill but failed 0/3 for without_skill. This is the specific, repeatable gap driving without_skill's lower expected-output and assertion scores — it appears without_skill consistently did not name or raise this specific finding ID, rather than failing intermittently.

Quality comparison: Only 1 of 3 pairs could be evaluated for quality (2 were skipped), so this comparison rests on limited data. In that one evaluated pair, with_skill was favored across all three criteria (accuracy, actionability, completeness), with medium average confidence. Given only one pair was assessed, this should be read as a single data point rather than a robust trend.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged 25s and $0.21 per run; without_skill averaged 17s and $0.14 per run — without_skill was faster and cheaper by a moderate margin (~8s, ~$0.07). Neither variant exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in the one runtime pair evaluated. Context window utilization was low for both (7.4% vs 4.8%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency across repeated runs: with_skill was rated fully "consistent" (score 3.0/3, high confidence). without_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" (score 2.67/3, high confidence), with 2 of 3 consistency dimensions fully consistent and 1 only mostly consistent — a small but real difference in run-to-run stability.

Overall, the data shows a consistent pattern: with_skill reliably identified and named the specific LLM-KB-001/HIGH-severity finding across all runs, while without_skill did not surface this finding in any run despite otherwise matching on related reasoning and safety-related assertions. This is offset by without_skill's lower runtime and cost. The quality-comparison and some expected-output confidence ratings are based on limited or medium-confidence data, so while the finding-naming gap appears robust and repeatable, the magnitude of the quality edge should be treated with some caution given the small sample.
